Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The ability to accurately evaluate and improve shooting performance is critical in basketball, affecting both individual player development and overall team success. Traditional methods of shot analysis often rely on manual observation and subjective evaluation, limiting their exactness and scalability. This research analyzes the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in basketball shot analysis, utilizing computer vision and machine learning to offer a more objective and data-driven approach. By processing video footage, the AI system retrieves key parameters such as player positioning, release angle, shooting arc, and ball trajectory. These metrics are used to assess shot quality and provide feedback, enabling players and coaches to make informed adjustments during training sessions. The study Tests the accuracy and efficiency of AI-based shot analysis compared to conventional methods, highlighting its potential to revolutionize basketball training and performance analysis. Results indicate that AI-enhanced analysis improves the precision of shot analyses and offers valuable insights for tailored skill development. This paper underscores the role of AI in advancing sports analytics and its Outcomes for enhancing athletic or users performance.

Chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide quick, fluent, and informative answers, but they sometimes generate incorrect or unsupported information known as hallucinations. These hallucinations can reduce user trust and create problems in areas such as education, healthcare, research, and customer support. Therefore, detecting and preventing hallucinated outputs is important for developing reliable and trustworthy AI systems. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a useful approach that retrieves relevant information from trusted sources before generating an answer. This retrieved information can be used to check whether the chatbot's response is accurate and supported by available evidence. However, RAG alone cannot completely prevent hallucinations because the generated answer may still contain incorrect facts, irrelevant information, or unsupported statements. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for detecting hallucinations in chatbot responses by combining information retrieval, evidence-based verification, and rule-based validation. The system compares the generated answer with retrieved information and identifies statements that are incorrect or lack sufficient supporting evidence. Based on the verification results, the system classifies the response as reliable or flagged. If the response contains unsupported information, the system can suggest corrections or prevent the answer from reaching the user without proper verification. The proposed approach aims to improve answer accuracy, reduce misleading information, and increase transparency in AI-based conversational systems. Although this framework offers a promising direction, its effectiveness depends on the quality of retrieved information, verification methods, and decision thresholds. Future evaluation should measure detection accuracy, response time, and computational cost. This approach can support the development of safer, more reliable, and trustworthy chatbots across different application areas.

Large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent but incorrect or fabricated statements, called hallucinations, which limits their use in education, healthcare and other high-stakes areas. Most existing safeguards act only after generation, and few correct errors automatically. This paper presents a structured narrative review of [N] verified sources published between [2022] and 2026, organized into seven themes: taxonomies, sampling-consistency detection, semantic-clustering methods, retrieval and fact-verification, internal-state detection, correction and integrated architectures, and evaluation practices. Black-box methods can detect hallucinations without external knowledge or model access, but only 8.8 % of reviewed systems combine detection and mitigation. Evidence relies heavily on question-answering benchmarks, small datasets, automatically generated labels and non-comparable metrics, and correction layers are rarely validated. The paper contributes a thematic synthesis, a comparison of [N] studies, a conceptual seven-layer self-correcting architecture and a prioritized research agenda.

Medical reports contain important health information, but their technical terminology and numerical results may be difficult for patients to understand. Recent studies have explored the use of large language models to simplify radiology reports, while also identifying concerns related to accuracy, omitted information, and potentially misleading explanations [1–3]. This paper proposes an AI-Based Intelligent Medical Report Understanding and Personal Health Management System designed to make medical information easier to understand and organize. The proposed framework will accept medical reports in PDF or image format, extract relevant text, and generate patient-friendly explanations while aiming to preserve important values, units, and reference ranges. A retrieval-based component is proposed to support explanations using reliable medical sources. Additional planned features include date-wise health-record organization, comparison of comparable report values, and reminders based on user-entered or clinician-provided instructions. The framework emphasizes privacy, factual consistency, and the distinction between educational information and professional medical advice. Its evaluation will examine text-extraction accuracy, preservation of medical information, factual consistency, readability, and usability after implementation. As the system has not yet been experimentally evaluated, this paper presents the proposed design and evaluation plan rather than measured performance results.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Solar energy has emerged as one of the most promising renewable energy sources due to its sustainability, abundance, and environmental benefits. However, the intermittent nature of solar power generation and system reliability challenges necessitate accurate forecasting and effective health monitoring techniques. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has significantly transformed solar energy systems by improving forecasting accuracy, fault detection, predictive maintenance, and energy storage optimization. This review paper explores recent advancements in AI-based solar power forecasting and health monitoring techniques, emphasizing models such as Support Vector Machine (SVM), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and hybrid frameworks. The study also examines AI-driven predictive maintenance approaches, including IoT-based monitoring, digital twin technologies, and thermal imaging methods for photovoltaic systems and battery energy storage systems. Furthermore, recent trends such as explainable AI, reinforcement learning, and smart grid integration are discussed. The paper highlights key challenges, including data quality, computational complexity, model generalization, and real-time deployment, while identifying future opportunities for intelligent and scalable solar energy management systems.

Healthcare intelligent systems employing wearable biosensors make possible continuous monitoring and clinical decision support. Wearable biosensors with ECG, PPG, body temperature, movement, and activity sensors record physiological data based on patients' health state. This chapter presents an adaptive AI-powered healthcare system designed for intelligent decision-making using machine learning and deep learning algorithms for analysis of physiological data streams and detection of risk factors associated with cardiovascular diseases, neurological conditions, and stress disorders. Learning methods facilitate the ability to adapt to patient data, while explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) ensures better understanding of model decisions. The proposed framework involves multimodal biosignal fusion, providing more accurate prediction results and giving real-time alerts and risk assessment to help physicians respond in time.

Global travel platforms compete in a market organised around data, algorithms, and network effects. Their success is commonly explained through data scale, technical sophistication, and platform economics. This chapter argues that these factors are necessary but not sufficient. Lasting AI-driven competitive advantage in global travel platforms is built on organisational behaviour (OB) micro foundations: cultures that treat experimentation as a routine activity, psychological safety that makes weak-signal learning possible, ambidextrous structures that reconcile exploration and exploitation, absorptive capacity that allows firms to recognise and assimilate external knowledge, human-AI teaming arrangements that combine algorithmic pattern recognition with human judgement, and leadership behaviours that align all of these with a coherent strategic narrative.

topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The travel and aviation industry has evolved from paper-based, isolated booking systems into a cloud-enabled, AI-driven ecosystem processing billions of passenger transactions each year. While this digital transformation has improved operational efficiency and customer experience, it has also expanded the industry's cyberattack surface, exposing airlines, online travel agencies, payment providers, and airport authorities to fraud, ransomware, identity theft, and other data-driven threats. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and blockchain-based identity frameworks collectively strengthen digital trust and reshape travel management. It traces the transition from centralized Global Distribution Systems to hybrid API-based architectures and from Web 2.0 identity silos to Web 3.0 self-sovereign identity. It concludes by highlighting emerging risks associated with generative AI and hybrid distribution ecosystems, alongside governance strategies for building resilient, future-ready travel infrastructures.

The decentralization, digitization, and decarbonization of energy systems have brought smart microgrids to the center of attention as we look at the modern power network. These local energy systems integrate distributed energy resources (DERs), energy storage, and advanced control techniques to develop reliability, resilience, and sustainability. However, these nonlinearities, complexity, and stochastic properties inherent in a smart microgrid are natural but demand more machine-like, adaptive modeling and simulation than is possible through rule-based models. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been added as the technology that turns out to address the challenges posed by the design, operation, and optimization of microgrids. Leveraging the strength of data-driven techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning, it is possible to use AI in order to construct dynamic, scalable, and predictive models that have the potential to be learnt either on the basis of historical or real-time data. Not only it is possible for such models to enhance the checking of the accuracy of the simulation, but they also help in making smart decisions regarding the prediction of loads, renewable integration, as well as fault identification and energy management systems. In this chapter, the authors&s; discussion focuses on AI-based approaches to smart microgrid model demonstration and simulation. It discusses significant AI strategies, simulation systems, and practical uses, as well as how AI can assist microgrids to be adaptive and independent in control under various conditions. Challenges and mitigation measures, the means of verification, and the prospects of integrating digital twins and multi-agent systems in order to render microgrids even more intelligent are also addressed. As the permeation of smart grids increases, one can expect modeling based on AI to potentially become a pillar of efficient, resilient, and sustainable power systems.

Phishing email remains a persistent cybersecurity threat, and large language models (LLMs) now allow fluent phishing text tobe produced at scale. This paper is a focused, literature-based comparative review of three recent studies that approach phishing emaildetection from different directions: a soft-voting ensemble with explainable-AI error analysis, a TF-IDF/SVM web platform with LIMEexplanations, and a stylometric classifier evaluated on GPT-4o-generated phishing emails alongside commercial spam filters. The studiesare compared by objective, dataset, feature family, model, evaluation protocol, reported metrics, explainability and stated limitations.Because the studies use different corpora and protocols, their reported figures are presented with attribution and are not ranked. Thecomparison suggests that content/structural detectors and stylometric detectors have been evaluated on largely disjoint data, so whethereither generalizes across conventional and AI-generated phishing is an open question raised by this review, not a verified research gap.The paper proposes a conceptual, unvalidated workflow that combines header/content/URL features, stylometric features, an ensembleclassifier and LIME-based analyst review, and specifies a future experimental protocol with hypotheses, cross-dataset tests and ablations.No new experimental results are reported.

Discussions about artificial intelligence in development often overlook how it reshapes everyday livelihoods in the Global South. This study examines how AI-driven virtual influencers (VIs) are transforming creative labour and digital visibility in Indonesia’s platform economy. Rather than autonomous technologies, VIs are produced through human–algorithm coordination shaped by platform logics and commercial imperatives. Drawing on 13 in-depth interviews with human influencers and one VI developer, this study shows how the expansion of VIs intensifies competition and creates increasing pressure for creators working with limited economic resources, unstable income, and self-funded production conditions. Thus, AI-driven systems reconfigure how income, visibility, and opportunities are distributed, contributing to unequal digital livelihoods. Simultaneously, VIs are designed to reflect local moral and aesthetic norms, revealing how global AI systems produce context-specific forms of inclusion and exclusion. These findings call for protection of creative workers, fair platform governance, and locally grounded AI policies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered design courses, but its use often stops at tool operation. Taking Landscape Architectonics, an undergraduate course in landscape architecture programs, as the vehicle, this paper builds a teaching framework for generative design that integrates four elements: research findings, design precedents, AI-based recognition and judgment, and AI generation. The core claim is simple. Teaching students to “use AI” means teaching them to run an evidence-constrained generative design chain. “AI-driven” therefore carries two meanings: at the tool level, AI executes generation; at the teaching level, evidence steers generation, and the work of teaching lies in leading students from the former toward the latter. Among the four elements, research findings and design precedents are static knowledge that travels across sites. Research findings supply criteria for what counts as good. Design precedents supply examples of what to do, distilled from 13 street design guidelines into 114 retrievable situation packages. AI-based recognition and AI generation produce dynamic outputs anchored to a specific site. Students mobilize these elements through three stages—reading the site, grounding the context, and giving form—and a chain of evidence disciplines each stage. The framework follows three design principles: complementary elements, partial embedding, and explicit judgment. Three classroom examples show how the framework operates. This paper focuses on framework construction and does not report learning-outcome data.

Artificial intelligence and security have motivated digital forensics and the paradigm shift in the form of threat identification. This chapter views AI solutions such as neural networks and deep learning as powerful tools for detecting, analysing and reducing cyber threats. The AI has significantly changed the traditional methods of security, namely, enabling the existence of real-time threat intelligence, automated incident response, and predictive analytics. However, this new technology has several problems, including adversarial attacks, explainability concerns, and ethical concerns. By discussing in detail the ambivalent nature of AI in cybersecurity as both an effective defensive mechanism and a potential attack source, the chapter considers both sources of current research and real-world use. Topics of application that are discussed are relevant, including locating malware, intrusion-finding systems, preventing phishing, and digital forensics. New developments such as generative AI, explainable AI, and quantum-resistant security are also discussed in the chapter. It further discusses the significance of balanced development, ensuring that the security solutions of the future digital infrastructure are robust, transparent, and virtuous, controlled by AI.

Artificial intelligence promises to improve drilling decisions, but field deployment remains constrained by delayed measurements, uncertain geology, inconsistent data quality and safety-critical operating limits. This critical review examines how measurement-while-drilling and logging while drilling information can support drilling rate optimisation adaptive well planning and predictive wellbore risk management within Saudi oil and gas operations. Thirty peer-reviewed publications issued between 2020 and 2025 were assessed through a structured, question led synthesis.The evidence was organized around measurement integrity, formation interpretation, optimisation architecture, trajectory revision, hazard prediction and deployment assurance. Published studies demonstrate substantial progress in rate - of - penetration forecasting, activity-aware influx detection and integrated geological-engineering planning. Nevertheless, model performance is generally assessed within particular fields or datasets; prospective validation, uncertainty calibration and evidence of avoided incidents remain less developed. The review proposes a bounded, human-supervised decision architecture in which physics-based constraints, data-quality controls and explicit operational authorisation separate algorithmic recommendations from drilling actions.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is widely adopted in fashion visual communication, yet imagery over-optimization causes product-image discrepancies and undermines consumer decisions. This study deconstructs three core characteristics of artificial intelligence-generated fashion imagery—visual realism, detail completeness, and style compatibility—and tests their impact on purchase intention via perceived authenticity and trust, with product price and consumer heterogeneity as moderators. Using a mixed-method approach (N = 845) and structural equation modeling, results confirm (1) the three characteristics positively influence purchase intention through direct risk reduction and indirect value identification, (2) trust plays dual mediating roles (direct and serial: artificial intelligence imagery → authenticity → trust → purchase intention), and (3) trust's mediation strengthens with higher prices (66.0% for high-price versus 39.6% for low-price products), and consumer segments differ in trust-building paths. This research enriches decision support system literature and offers actionable strategies for fashion brands.

Background AI chatbots are increasingly used for health and exercise information. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a common exercise topic, yet the quality, transparency, and readability of chatbot-generated HIIT information have not been systematically compared under a standardized testing protocol. Objective To compare selected dimensions of quality, transparency, and readability in HIIT-related responses generated by ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity, and to evaluate readability against a prespecified sixth-grade benchmark for public-facing health information. Methods This cross-sectional comparative content analysis was conducted in August 2026. Google Trends was used to identify HIIT-related search terms worldwide over the preceding 5 years. Of 29 candidate terms, 14 were retained after predefined screening, and each term was submitted once to each of four chatbots, yielding 56 responses. Two reviewers, both holding doctoral degrees in sports science, independently evaluated all responses using DISCERN, EQIP, the JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS, which assessed complementary dimensions of information quality, usability, transparency, and overall usefulness. Inter-rater reliability was assessed before adjudication. Six readability indices were calculated. Because the same 14 queries were evaluated across all four chatbots, overall differences were tested using Friedman tests; significant results were followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Kendall’s W was reported as the overall effect-size measure. Results Perplexity-generated responses had the highest median scores for DISCERN [51.50 (47.50, 53.75)], EQIP [75.00 (70.00, 80.00)], JAMA [1.00 (1.00, 1.00)], and GQS [4.00 (4.00, 4.00)]. Friedman tests showed significant differences across chatbots for DISCERN (χ 2 = 27.98, p < 0.001, W = 0.666), EQIP (χ 2 = 25.74, p < 0.001, W = 0.613), JAMA (χ 2 = 35.40, p < 0.001, W = 0.843), and GQS (χ 2 = 21.15, p < 0.001, W = 0.504). None of the four chatbots met the prespecified sixth-grade readability benchmark across the evaluated indices. Conclusion Under this specific testing protocol, HIIT-related responses generated by the four chatbots differed in the evaluated dimensions of information quality and transparency, with Perplexity-generated responses receiving higher median scores on all four assessment instruments. These scores should not be interpreted as direct evidence of factual accuracy, citation accuracy, or clinical safety, which were not independently assessed. None of the evaluated chatbot-generated responses met the prespecified readability benchmark.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (AI)-guided framework for predicting compressive strength (CS) and assessing the sustainability of ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) mixtures incorporating supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), nano-additives, and sustainable waste-derived constituents. A database containing 1990 experimental records of 28-day CS was compiled from the literature. Three tree-based machine learning algorithms, namely Extra Trees Regressor (ETR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), together with stacked ensemble models, were developed and optimized using the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). Based on outcomes, among all developed models, the SM-4 (XGB+ETR+LGBM) model achieved the best overall testing performance with an R² of 0.885, RMSE of 12.40 MPa, MAE of 8.80 MPa, MAPE of 5.94%, and RMSRE of 8.37%. SHAP analyses identified curing temperature, fiber dosage, silica fume content, cement dosage, and water content as the most influential predictors. Cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA)-based analyses further evaluated carbon emissions, embodied energy, and material cost. Additionally, a multi-objective inverse-design framework coupled the best-performing stacked model with NSGA-II and TOPSIS to identify UHPC mixture proportions for eight CS targets from 130 to 200 MPa while considering sustainability indicators and mixture-design requirements. Selected mixtures were produced and experimentally tested to compare measured CS with predictions and prescribed targets. Finally, an AI-guided graphical user interface (GUI) was developed for rapid CS prediction and sustainability assessment. The proposed framework integrates interpretable prediction, sustainability assessment, and multi-objective optimization to identify UHPC mixtures for prescribed strength targets, with experimental validation supporting practical mixture-design applications.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the global travel industry by enhancing personalization, operational efficiency, and strategic competitiveness. This chapter synthesizes contemporary literature to examine AI applications in customer experience, revenue management, supply chain optimization, destination management, and risk management. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, it explains how AI-enabled resources, data-driven capabilities, and organizational learning create sustainable competitive advantage. The chapter also discusses ethical, regulatory, and workforce implications associated with AI adoption. By integrating strategic management theories with practical AI applications across airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, and destination management organizations, the chapter provides a comprehensive perspective on how AI drives innovation, organizational resilience, and long-term competitiveness in the global travel industry.

Women's safety is still an everyday concern in public places, workplaces and homes, and most tools in use today depend on the victim pressing a button at the worst possible moment. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers another route: listening for distress in the surroundings, combining it with other signals, and forecasting where and when the risk is highest. This paper reviews 15 IEEE-published sources from 2014 to 2024 that relate to this idea. They cover IoT-based safety devices, scream and distress detection from audio, speech emotion and fear recognition, multimodal wearable systems, crime hotspot prediction, and edge and privacy-preserving deployment. The review finds that the audio models report accuracies between 92% and 100% on the datasets they were tested on, while the one multimodal wearable study that tested fear recognition on unseen subjects reached 63.61%. Crime-prediction methods are mature at city level but are rarely linked to women-specific incidents or to live sensing. Most studies rely on small, public or acted data, say little about false alarms, response delay and battery use, and give limited attention to privacy, accents and noisy streets. The paper contributes a comparison of eleven representative works, a conceptual seven-layer architecture that joins on-device audio detection with predictive risk analytics, and a prioritised list of research gaps. The architecture is conceptual and has not been tested experimentally.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: This chapter analyses the strategic incorporation of artificial intelligence technology into renewable energy systems to enhance energy security, operational efficiency, and long-term sustainability. This chapter aims to examine how intelligent energy management systems, machine learning algorithms, smart grids, decentralized microgrids, and Internet of Things (IoT) networks can enhance the performance and resilience of renewable energy systems. This chapter places emphasis on predictive analytics, battery management, solar forecasting, digital twins, and autonomous energy optimization. The chapter examines the economic, environmental, and technological ramifications of intelligent energy systems, emphasizing their capacity to minimize energy losses, improve system reliability, facilitate decentralized electrification, and expedite sustainable energy transitions towards enhanced national energy independence.

Metaverse technologies let users interact inside virtual environments, where each user is represented by an avatar that carries their digital identity. These environments now attract many application domains, and these domains do not all need the same level of security. Conventional authentication methods do not fit them well. They ignore the continuity of user activity during a session and do not exploit the metaverse's rich set of interaction modalities, far broader than in 2D systems, through which an avatar continuously produces voice, head movement, gaze, and others. Moreover, they cannot adjust to different security levels within the same environment. Therefore, continuous, non-intrusive and adaptive authentication is needed. We first review existing avatar authentication approaches, organize them into three categories, and draw out the limitations a solution must address. Building on this, we propose an AI-driven continuous multimodal authentication framework for the metaverse. The framework reads behavioral biometrics from several interaction modalities and authenticates the user through their avatar without breaking immersion. The security level is continuously adjusted to the context of the session, using an adaptive control mechanism that weighs scene sensitivity, risk, and trust. A generative AI component builds context-aware authentication scenarios that adjust to the required security level and to the sensitivity of the scene. We evaluate the framework in two ways: a comparison against existing work, and a scenario-based analysis. The comparison shows that our framework integrates capabilities that previous approaches generally address separately, while the scenario-based analysis illustrates its intended operation and its internal consistency with respect to adaptivity and context-awareness.

This study aims to identify the obstacles faced by prospective couples in fulfilling the administrative requirements for marriage registration at the Tembalang Religious Affairs Office (KUA) in Semarang City, analyze the causal factors, and formulate appropriate solutions to overcome them. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through interviews, questionnaires, and observation involving 7 KUA staff members and 20 prospective couples. Data analysis was conducted using a descriptive-analytical method based on the Miles and Huberman interactive model, strengthened by triangulation techniques. The findings reveal that the main obstacles include incomplete N1–N5 documents, birth certificates, health certificates, parents’ marriage books, outdated identity cards and family cards, commander’s permission for TNI/Polri members, and guardian-related issues due to parental divorce. Contributing factors include limited information, prospective couples’ lack of thoroughness, processes at other institutions, and family-related problems. In addition, the poorly positioned physical information media and non-ergonomic spatial layout exacerbate information asymmetry. This study recommends strengthening public education, improving spatial layout, and optimizing information media to enhance the effectiveness of marriage registration services.

Undergraduate research faces unprecedented challenges in the digital era, as exponentially growing data increasingly shapes the university ecosystem. However, artificial intelligence, particularly tools such as ChatGPT, offers significant opportunities to address this transformation. Effective use requires advanced competencies in generating, acquiring, storing, and analyzing data. In response, this study developed and validated a new Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale to assess undergraduate students’ competencies in research contexts. This study examined the relationship between Big Data socio-technical competencies and undergraduate students' academic use of ChatGPT, as well as the underlying meta-skills for using AI in research. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (QUAN → qual) was adopted, involving 418 undergraduate students. We used two measurement instruments: the newly developed and validated Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale and a scale measuring the academic use of ChatGPT; both showed high internal consistency, along with a semi-structured interview protocol. The findings show that Big Data competencies were generally low, whereas the academic use of ChatGPT for research was predominantly medium to high. Structural equation modeling revealed that socio-technical competencies in Big Data positively and significantly predict the academic use of ChatGPT (β = 0.269, p < .001). The qualitative phase identified nine Artificial Intelligence Meta-Skills for Undergraduate Research: (1) Critical Data Literacy, (2) Critical Thinking, (3) Epistemic Data Management, (4) Evidence-Based Decision-Making, (5) Critical Data Communication, (6) Metacognitive Regulation, (7) Emotional Self-Regulation, (8) Responsible Human–AI Agency, and (9) Ethical Reasoning. The study discusses educational implications and practical applications.

Occupational health and safety risk assessment (OHSRA) is a critical activity to identify and analyze the risk of occupational hazards for ensuring the safety of workers, and then take measures to control occupational risk at a tolerable level. In this study, an improved OHSRA model based on consensus analysis and the measurement of alternatives and ranking according to compromise solution (MARCOS) method is introduced to assess and prioritize the risk of occupational hazards under linguistic D numbers (LDNs) environment. First, the LDNs are employed to express the uncertain or hesitant risk assessments of occupational hazards provided by experts. Second, an improved minimum conflict consensus method (MCCM) is adopted to coordinate the conflict opinions among experts considering their conflicting degrees. Then, the MARCOS method is modified to determine the risk ranking of occupational hazards. Finally, an illustrative hospital-based application focusing on medical staff occupational hazards is presented to show the implementation procedure of the proposed OHSRA model. Sensitivity and comparative analyses are further conducted to examine the robustness of the results within this specific application context.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose Rare financial-distress events create a distinctive decision-support problem in e-commerce logistics ecosystems: missing a distressed partner can be costly, yet excessive alerts can overwhelm limited human review capacity. This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs), when provided with mechanism-structured financial information, can support rare-event screening under extreme class imbalance. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share transportation and logistics firms as an empirical proxy for logistics-partner risk monitoring, we construct a two-year-ahead financial-distress prediction task containing 880 firm-year observations from feature years 2013–2022, including 12 ST/*ST cases. All conventional machine-learning (ML) models and eight zero-shot LLMs are evaluated on the same chronological holdout sample of 176 observations, including four distress cases. We develop Financial Narrative Serialization (FNS) to organize 21 financial and textual indicators into interpretable financial contexts and combine it with a Temporal Context-Aware Chain-of-Thought (TCA-CoT) protocol that structures the assessment around liquidity stress, inefficient expansion, and fundamental deterioration. ML benchmarks include unweighted learning, cost-sensitive learning, enhanced features, mechanism-feature ablation, and threshold sensitivity. Findings Extreme class imbalance produces markedly different screening behaviors across models. At a 0.5 reference threshold, the most selective cost-sensitive ML ensemble identifies two of four distress cases while generating three false positives; lower thresholds can recover additional distress cases but may eventually approach an all-alert rule. TCA-CoT increases recall for five of the eight LLMs and leaves recall unchanged for three. For Qwen-Turbo, recall rises from 0.50 to 1.00 as the number of flagged observations increases from 33 to 104. The additional false-positive observations exhibit, on average, weaker liquidity, higher leverage, poorer operating cash-flow quality, and lower profitability than true negatives. These results indicate that structured prompting can shift the LLM screening boundary toward financially vulnerable observations, although broader risk coverage increases the burden of secondary review. Practical implications The findings support a layered screening workflow in which AI prioritizes potentially vulnerable firms for subsequent human assessment. Model selection should therefore reflect the organization’s tolerance for missed risks and its available review capacity rather than rely on a single predictive metric. Originality/value This study develops a mechanism-structured financial representation for zero-shot LLM screening and evaluates ML and LLM approaches in a common rare-event environment. It further introduces a decision-support perspective that jointly considers distress coverage, false alarms, and human review volume.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly present in primary mathematics classrooms, yet their educational value is widely argued to depend on how teachers use them. Existing models explain parts of this problem: AI-TPACK describes the knowledge teachers need, teacher-in-the-loop and human-centred AI models describe how control is shared between teachers and systems, and orchestration research describes how teachers coordinate classroom activity. What remains under-theorised is the pathway linking the way open distance e-learning (ODeL) professional development builds teachers’ capacity to its enactment when AI scaffolds learners’ problem-solving. This conceptual article asks: through which mechanisms, and under which conditions, can ODeL-based professional development be expected to enable teacher-facilitated human–AI collaboration that supports primary learners’ mathematical problem-solving? The analysis combined an integrative review of peer-reviewed and selected grey literature with theory synthesis: sources were identified through structured database searches, screened against pre-specified criteria, coded for constructs, mechanisms and boundary conditions, and organised by level of analysis. The primary context is South African primary schooling (Grades 1–7) and low-bandwidth, predominantly asynchronous ODeL. Positioning four perspectives within a multilevel meta-model, Intelligent-TPACK at the teacher level, Zone of Proximal Development scaffolding and social constructivism at the interaction and classroom levels, and Polya’s heuristic as an analytic lens at the learner level, with transactional distance theory at the programme level, I propose a three-layer framework that distinguishes inputs, mechanisms, practices and outcomes, and derive seven testable propositions. These include teacher orchestration as a mediator between AI-TPACK and scaffolding quality; infrastructure readiness, learner age, language, and AI type as moderators; and governance and children’s rights as cross-cutting boundary conditions. Unlike models that specify teacher knowledge or the division of control alone, the framework specifies the professional development pathway through which human–AI collaboration is expected to benefit learners. I propose that well-designed ODeL professional development is an enabling condition for such benefit, not a guarantee of it, and close with implementation and evaluation indicators for teacher educators, policymakers, school leaders, researchers and learners.

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management and safety culture in relation to employee performance at PT XYZ Purwakarta. Occupational Health and Safety is an essential aspect of industrial operations because it helps protect employees from workplace accidents, occupational hazards, and potential health problems. Effective OHS management also supports the creation of a safe, comfortable, and productive working environment. The implementation of OHS at PT XYZ includes the provision of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), regular safety training for both new and existing employees, and routine supervision to ensure compliance with established Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). These measures are intended to increase employee awareness, reduce workplace risks, and encourage safe working practices. Furthermore, a strong safety culture plays an important role in shaping employee behavior and improving individual responsibility for workplace safety. Employees who understand the importance of safety procedures are more likely to comply with regulations, identify potential hazards, and contribute to accident prevention. However, the effectiveness of OHS management still requires continuous improvement, particularly through enhanced safety knowledge, consistent supervision, and greater employee participation in safety-related activities. Human negligence remains a potential risk factor that must be addressed through education, communication, and regular evaluation. Overall, effective OHS management combined with a positive safety culture can contribute to workplace safety, employee well-being, operational stability, and improved employee performance at PT XYZ Purwakarta

documents.abstract: This article presents a systematic analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods applied to the optimization of energy system stability. Deep learning architectures for forecasting electricity demand and renewable energy generation, reinforcement learning algorithms for microgrid control, the concept of digital twins, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods are examined. The application of hybrid models reduces forecasting errors by 20–35% over ultra-short-term forecasting horizons ranging from several minutes to several hours. The transition to probabilistic forecasting reduces balancing costs by 8–15%, while the use of digital twins decreases operating costs by 15–25%. Current challenges limiting the implementation of intelligent technologies in the energy sector are identified, and priority areas for further research are outlined. The results are systematized in comparative tables suitable for practical use when selecting appropriate methodological tools.

Aiming at the bottleneck problems of path explosion and low efficiency of constraint solving faced by dynamic symbolic execution (DSE) in large-scale Web software systems, this paper applies a DSE and test coverage enhancement method combined with artificial intelligence (AI). Firstly, an Actor-Critic dual network model is constructed based on the PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) algorithm. The Actor network outputs the probability distribution of path selection, and the Critic network evaluates the value of path state. Secondly, the path priority sorting strategy is updated through the generalized advantage estimation and pruning mechanism, and the path depth threshold is gradually increased by combining curriculum learning. The key branch priority solving strategy is applied to optimize the efficiency of constraint solving. Finally, after each round of symbolic execution, the coverage increment is used as a reward signal to update the model parameters online and dynamically optimize the path exploration strategy. Experimental results show that this method significantly improves the efficiency of path exploration (the number of paths reaches 225 and 216, respectively) and test coverage (74.9% and 73.4%) on large-scale Web systems, with an average solution success rate of 79.8% and an average vulnerability detection rate of 88%. It has good vulnerability detection capabilities and resource adaptability, and provides an efficient and scalable new paradigm for automated testing of complex systems.

Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education. Its educational effects in nursing remain uncertain. Purpose: To evaluate the effects of using GenAI in teaching nursing. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to July 2026. Standardized mean differences and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were pooled using random-effects models. Heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses, meta-regression, and small-study effects were explored. Results: Seventeen studies involving 1456 participants were included. GenAI-integrated teaching was associated with higher knowledge scores (standardized mean differences 0.53, 95% CI 0.03-1.04), practice-related scores (SMD 1.25, 95% CI 0.23-2.28), and teaching satisfaction (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.02-1.13). Attitudes, competency, and self-efficacy did not differ significantly. Meta-regression findings were exploratory. Conclusions: GenAI-integrated teaching may improve knowledge, practice-related performance, and satisfaction in nursing education. However, extreme heterogeneity and sensitivity to individual studies limit confidence in the magnitude and reproducibility of these effects. GenAI should be used as a supervised pedagogical adjunct pending high-quality trials.

documents.abstract: Universities have a wide range of expertise, but identifying the right people for complex, cross-disciplinary opportunities can be difficult. Expertise is often spread across faculties, research centres and different institutional systems. When funding and partnership opportunities have short response periods, those supporting team formation may rely on familiar networks and people with relevant but less obvious capabilities. UTS TeamBuilder is an AI-assisted tool that helps people find the right researchers, explore expertise across the university, and form teams around new opportunities. Rather than simply producing a list of names, the tool supports the broader team formation process, from framing the challenge and exploring institutional capability to preparing introductions and facilitating early conversations. The tool brings together evidence from multiple institutional sources, including researcher profiles, publication abstracts, research projects, proposals and staff bios. It uses natural language processing, network analysis, interactive visualization and generative AI to help users explore expertise, assess possible team combinations, and understand the evidence behind suggestions. Outputs can include expertise landscapes, preliminary team propositions, personalised invitations and prompts to support early team conversations. A key principle behind the tool is that AI should support, rather than replace, human judgement. Users can inspect the visualizations and analysis used by the AI, refine the researcher pool, explore proposed team members, and adjust the direction of the analysis. TeamBuilder therefore broadens the user’s field of view and provides informed starting points, while leaving decisions about team composition and suitability with the human user.

This chapter offers an overview of widely used artificial intelligence terminology to support informed engagement in art therapy. As AI systems evolve rapidly, ongoing AI literacy combined with digital humility helps practitioners, students, and educators evaluate emerging tools in ways that align with professional ethics. The chapter defines core concepts such as artificial intelligence, large language models, chatbot, agent, and deep learning, alongside evolving social and policy terms including AI slop and responsible AI. It situates these terms within art therapy practice and broader societal contexts. The chapter underscores that AI systems are computational tools with significant transformative capacity and therefore require ethical discernment. Their outputs differ fundamentally from human creativity and lived experience and must be approached with careful clinical judgment, reflective practice, and professional accountability.

documents.abstract: Abstract Complicated urinary tract infection associated with urinary stone disease remains clinically challenging because obstruction, infected stones, delayed microbiological confirmation, and antimicrobial resistance may converge in the same patient. Artificial intelligence can support this pathway when it is framed as clinical risk integration rather than isolated image recognition. We conducted a structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 July 2026, supplemented by reference chaining and relevant clinical and reporting guidelines. The synthesis distinguishes direct evidence in stone-associated infection and perioperative infectious outcomes from indirect evidence in stone detection, volumetry, recurrence, and general UTI stewardship. Radiomics and machine learning studies show promising discrimination, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and frequently lacks external validation, complete calibration reporting, and prospective impact assessment. Artificial intelligence should therefore be treated as an adjunct to urological assessment, cultures, imaging, antimicrobial stewardship, and timely source control. For African settings, pragmatic validation must account for local resistance patterns, uneven access to CT and microbiology, referral delays, infrastructure, and the availability of urgent drainage.

documents.abstract: This study examines the nexus between digital technology adoption and Sustainable Supply Chain Management, focusing on their combined impact on sustainability performance. By bridging the domains of digital transformation and sustainability, the research advances a comprehensive conceptual framework that captures the effects of Industry 4.0 technologies, specifically the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, and blockchain, on sustainable supply chain outcomes. The proposed model posits that digital technology adoption enhances sustainability performance indirectly through improved supply chain transparency, with this relationship moderated by the presence of a skilled workforce. Grounded in a thorough review of contemporary literature, the study highlights the role of Industry 4.0 technologies in promoting eco-efficient production and logistics, the contribution of blockchain to strengthening transparency, and the optimization of resource utilization through AI. An empirical quantitative study based on survey data collected from 250 manufacturing firms provides evidence of the partial mediation effect of transparency and validates the moderating influence of human capital in reinforcing the relationship between digital transformation and sustainability. The findings offer novel theoretical insights into the mechanisms linking digital adoption to SSCM and yield practical implications for managers seeking to leverage Industry 4.0 technologies for sustainability objectives. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future research to further advance the digital–sustainability interface.

documents.abstract: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and doctrinal authority in the context of the Church of Ghana. The increasing use of AI in sermon preparation, biblical interpretation, theological research, and religious communication has raised important theological and ethical concerns regarding the integrity of Christian doctrine and the legitimacy of machine-assisted theological content. The study specifically explored how AI influences theological interpretation, the ethical issues associated with AI-generated religious content, and how churches should respond to AI-driven theological tools. The study was underpinned by Hermeneutical Theory and Technological Determinism Theory and grounded in the interpretivist paradigm. It used a qualitative research approach with a phenomenological research design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with nineteen purposively selected participants, including pastors, church leaders, seminary lecturers, theological educators, and theological students. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that AI is increasingly being used in sermon structuring, biblical explanation, theological research, contextual communication, and comparative doctrinal synthesis. However, the study also found that AI-generated religious content raises serious concerns related to doctrinal inconsistency, authorship and authenticity, overdependence, misinformation, and spiritual disconnection. The study concludes that while AI may serve as a useful assistive tool in ministry and theological education, it cannot function as a source of doctrinal authority. The paper recommends doctrinal oversight, digital theological literacy, and ethical guidelines for the use of responsible AI in Christian contexts.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper explores the use and perception of artificial intelligence in the context of sustainability in nature-based tourism (NBT) destinations, examining the interplay among ecological conservation, visitor experience and community well-being through a Tourism Social–Ecological–Technological Systems framework. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design synthesized 44 peer-reviewed studies identified via Scopus and Web of Science. Bibliometric co-occurrence mapping in VOSviewer first established macro-level structural clusters, which directly seeded the coding framework for deductive–inductive thematic analysis in NVivo with inter-rater reliability checks. The study integrated findings from both phases to derive the final socio-technical dimensions. Findings The integrated analysis identified three core clusters: sociotechnical sustainability demonstrates that smart and ambient systems optimize mobility, monitor ecological impacts and support visitor management, though realization depends on institutional capacity and data governance; robotics and automation indicates that while autonomous systems improve operational resilience and resource efficiency, they introduce risks of experiential dehumanization, labour displacement and ethical concerns and social-ecological and human dimensions highlights AI’s capacity to foster environmental stewardship and local livelihoods, while cautioning against algorithmic standardization that privileges commodified, image-driven experiences over low-impact, context-specific practices. Originality/value This study is among the first to synthesize AI–sustainability research in NBT through a multi-dimensional Tourism Social-Ecological-Technological Systems perspective, uncovering systemic synergies and socio-technical tensions to guide responsible technological interventions in fragile destinations.

Abstract: AI is flooding into India's job market faster than most legislative frameworks can keep up with. This review draws together nineteen peer-reviewed publications, working papers and institutional reports, mostly published between 2023 and 2026, in order to evaluate what is empirically known about the employment effects of AI in India, as opposed to what is anticipated or assumed. The review finds that empirical evidence is still concentrated in India's formal services sector, where AI-related hiring has skyrocketed since 2016 and appears to have reduced demand for high-skilled managerial and analytical roles rather than low-skilled ones. Most of the Indian workers are engaged in manufacturing, agriculture and the informal economy, all of which have little evidence largely based on projections and not empirical. The review categorises the literature based on four recurring mechanisms: task displacement, task reinstatement, productivity-driven labour demand and skill polarisation. Distributional data show AI exposure in India is stratified by caste, gender and educational attainment. The most urgent void in Indian literature is sector-specific, worker-level empirical research outside of IT services. documents.abstract: Modern electrical networks face growing operational demands as electricity consumption rises and renewable generation, distributed resources, and electric vehicles become more common. Artificial intelligence (AI) can learn useful relationships from operating records and simulated data, supporting tasks such as demand prediction, fault identification, state estimation, stability screening, and energy scheduling. This review organizes reported AI techniques and applications in both large interconnected grids and smaller power systems. It considers rule-based and fuzzy approaches alongside machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and newer foundation-model methods. The literature suggests that AI may accelerate selected analyses and provide flexible decision support, but dependable performance still relies on representative data, generalization, explainability, cyber protection, and real-world validation. A staged approach that combines AI with engineering models and expert oversight is outlined. This paper synthesizes existing studies and does not claim new experimental results..

Background: The use of digital health technologies, such as chatbots and virtual assistants based on artificial intelligence, has grown significantly in maternal health. These tools have been applied at different stages of the pregnancy and postpartum cycle, with emphasis on health education, risk monitoring, breastfeeding support, and mental healthcare. Despite their potential, challenges remain regarding clinical effectiveness, equity of access, and ethical safety. The aim of this study was to map the available evidence regarding the applications of artificial intelligence in pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care, with particular emphasis on conversational agents, virtual assistants, machine learning models, and clinical decision support systems, as well as their potential benefits, limitations, ethical implications, and implementation challenges. Methods: A scoping review was conducted between August and September 2025 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Nursing Database, Latin American and Caribbean Literature in Health Sciences, and Google Scholar. Original articles, reviews, experience reports, and theoretical reflections published in Portuguese, English, or Spanish that addressed the use of digital tools based on artificial intelligence in the pregnancy and postpartum cycle were included. The analysis of the studies was organized into five thematic axes: applications in prenatal care; support during childbirth; postpartum monitoring and breastfeeding; perinatal mental health; and ethical, technical, and implementation challenges. Results: The search identified 6230 records, of which 13 studies were included. Findings indicate that chatbots and virtual assistants show good acceptability, promote health education, and contribute to the early detection of physical and emotional risks. However, most of the studies are exploratory, with methodological limitations, lack of clinical trials, and limited validation in socially vulnerable contexts. Conclusions: Chatbots and artificial intelligence tools are promising resources for perinatal care, particularly as a complement to face-to-face attention. Their consolidation requires robust studies, cost-effectiveness assessments, and public policies that ensure equity and digital inclusion.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned at the intersection of business transformation and sustainable development. Its capacity to identify patterns in large datasets, forecast demand and risk, automate routine processes, support product innovation, and improve resource allocation creates opportunities to enhance organizational performance while addressing environmental and social priorities. Yet these outcomes are not automatic: AI can reproduce bias, intensify surveillance, displace or transform work, widen digital inequalities, and consume substantial energy and material resources. This conceptual study synthesizes the supplied literature review on AI-enabled sustainability, digital transformation, innovation, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It develops an integrated framework in which AI capabilities influence sustainable business transformation through three complementary mechanisms: operational and resource optimization, innovation capability, and data-driven decision-making. The proposed framework links AI adoption with economic, environmental, and social sustainability through digital infrastructure, workforce skills, organizational readiness, and collaboration. Responsible governance, fairness, accountability, and data protection ensure ethical implementation. AI-driven sustainability requires strategic alignment, organizational learning, and responsible practices to achieve measurable business transformation and sustainable outcomes. As a conceptual paper, it does not claim empirical validation; instead, it offers propositions and a research agenda for future survey, case-study, and structural-equation modelling research.

documents.abstract: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.

Introduction: Gastrointestinal disorders involve interacting digestive, emotional, sleep, and behavioral factors requiring longitudinal assessment. Objective: To evaluate 12-week feasibility, engagement, and clinical associations of a mobile AI-driven mental health assistant in adults with gastrointestinal disorders. Methods: This prospective comparative study enrolled 186 Venezuelan adults with irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, functional dyspepsia, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Participants were assigned to a mobile AI assistant plus standard medical care (n=94) or standard medical care (n=92). The intervention combined conversational support, journaling, and emotional self-reports with required wearable-based monitoring (e.g., smartwatch and smart ring). Both groups underwent assessment of sleep, resting heart rate, nocturnal heart-rate variability, and daily steps. The primary outcome was symptomatic days per week. GAD-7 and PHQ-9 assessed anxiety and depression; adjusted differences included 95% confidence intervals. Results: Participant retention was 91.5% in the intervention group and 85.9% in the standard medical care group, with fewer symptomatic days, reduced anxiety and depression, and 28 additional minutes of sleep nightly. Resting heartrate decreased by 3.6 beats/min and nocturnal RMSSD increased by 5.1 ms relative to comparison; both confidence intervals excluded zero. Daily-step differences were nonsignificant. Daily check-in completion among enrolled participants was 74.8%. Conclusions: The mobile AI intervention was associated with improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms, emotional outcomes, sleep, and autonomic measures.ESCUCHE EL RESUMEN HANCIENDO CLIC EN EL IDIOMA DE SU PREFERENCIA:EspañolEnglishPortugués Japones

Lifestyle counseling is central to cardiovascular prevention, yet recommendations may be difficult to communicate within routine consultations and to translate into feasible daily actions. This perspective proposes a clinician supervised framework in which artificial intelligence helps draft patient readable lifestyle plans from explicitly approved clinical instructions. The framework separates deterministic safety rules and curated clinical content from language generation; a template system without machine learning is recognized as a valid alternative. Personalization is limited to clinician verified information and patient stated preferences, including language, food affordability, and practical access to physical activity. Proposed safeguards include data minimization, version controlled source material, documented review, patient clarification, and escalation when inputs are incomplete or conflicting. Particular attention is given to professional accountability, health literacy, digital exclusion, and the possibility that fluent drafts encourage superficial verification. Lifestyle advice is not assumed to be inherently safe, especially in patients with multimorbidity. This article presents a conceptual proposal rather than an evaluated intervention or systematic review. A staged research agenda compares the approach with high quality nonautomated counseling materials and measures safety, comprehension, clinician workload, equity, and sustained behavior change. Any benefit remains to be established empirically; the intended contribution is a testable model of accountable health communication rather than a claim of improved cardiovascular outcomes.

documents.abstract: Purpose:This study examined undergraduate nursing students’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence and their readiness for medical artificial intelligence, as well as the factors associated with AI readiness.Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional design was employed. Two hundred and fifty undergraduate nursing students at a nursing faculty in western Türkiye participated during the 2025–2026 academic year. Three instruments were administered: a Participant Information Form, the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students.Results: The Positive General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale yielded a mean of 3.88 ± 0.66, the Negative General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale 3.26 ± 0.87, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students 74.29 ± 13.43. Academic year was significantly associated with AI readiness. One-way ANOVA showed significant differences across year groups (F = 3.450; p = 0.012; η² = 0.040), with fourth-year students scoring higher than second-year students. In the multiple linear regression analysis, both second-year (β = −0.156, p = 0.014) and third-year (β = −0.143, p = 0.024) students had significantly lower readiness scores compared with fourth-year students. A moderate positive correlation was observed between positive AI attitudes and readiness scores(r = 0.430; p < 0.01). Positive attitudes toward AI and self-reported computer skills emerged as the strongest independent factors associated with readiness.Conclusion: Nursing students displayed generally favorable attitudes toward AI, yet readiness levels varied across academic years. Attitude and readiness, while correlated, appear to be distinct constructs. These findings highlight the need for intentional, practice-oriented integration of AI competencies into undergraduate nursing curricula.

documents.abstract: As a result of the blistering emergence of the digital ecosystem, the cases of cybercrime have risen at an alarming rate, and it is a significant challenge to all law enforcement agencies and forensic investigators. Traditional investigation techniques are often not adequate to manage the volume, scope, and rate of the existing cyber threats. This chapter, Artificial Intelligence for Cybercrime Investigation and Forensics, talks of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its use in investigating and preventing cybercrimes in terms of how automation, predictive modeling, and smart data interpretation will enable easier identification and solve cybercrime cases. It discusses various AI paradigms, such as Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing, and Computer Vision, which can help to raise the accuracy and efficiency of forensics. The other area that the chapter covers is the use of AI to identify threats, profile behaviors, authenticate evidence, and even create digital traces, and this provides an overall picture of how AI has been impacting the improvement of cyber justice systems. Furthermore, it describes significant ethical, legal, and technical challenges, including the privacy of data, bias of algorithms, and the application of AI-generated evidence in a court of justice. The chapter gives the readers a glimpse of a future where smart, transparent, and autonomous AI-driven forensic systems can assist in combating the evolving digital threats and still provide the investigations with fairness, accountability, and trust in the online investigations.

Sports talent identification (TID) seeks to detect and select athletes with exceptional potential, but conventional practice relies heavily on coach and scout judgement and is exposed to relative age effects, differences in biological maturation and small-sample intuition. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), is increasingly proposed as a decision-support tool that can integrate anthropometric, physical, technical, psychosocial and match-tracking data. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified peer-reviewed studies, prioritising 2019–2026 publications, that apply AI to talent selection, performance prediction, playing-position classification, athlete profiling and scouting. The review examines three connected themes: data sources (field tests, match and tracking data, psychosocial measures, maturation indicators and video), learning methods (penalised regression, tree ensembles, support vector machines, neural networks and unsupervised clustering), and validation and deployment practice. The literature shows that models reach moderate to high internal discrimination, with area under the ROC curve (AUC) values reported from about 0.58 to 0.96 in a recent systematic review, while very high accuracies are usually reported for small or augmented datasets without external validation. Most studies are male-dominated, soccer-dominated and single-club, and few report calibration, fairness audits or prospective testing. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a conceptual athlete-to-decision architecture that links multi-source data acquisition, age- and maturation-aware modelling, calibrated and explainable prediction, human-in-the-loop decision support and external validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.

documents.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of emerging efforts to apply artificial intelligence (AI) to mental health assessment, including art-based assessment. As art therapy assessment requires ongoing, integrative, and attentive clinical judgment, the often opaque or “black box” nature of AI systems that analyze large datasets raises practical and ethical questions. The chapter reviews the feasibility, risks, and limitations of AI-enabled tools for art-based assessment and centers on a conversation with Taeeun Kim, an art therapist and researcher based in South Korea who contributed to the development of AI assessment applications for art therapy practice and education. Drawing on an in-depth interview with Kim, alongside established frameworks for evaluating AI tools in mental health, the chapter critically examines key ethical and clinical considerations. It concludes with practical recommendations and preliminary guidelines for art therapists and related professionals who may encounter, evaluate, or seek to develop AI-enabled assessment tools, with particular attention to protecting client agency, clinical judgment, cultural understanding, and contextual awareness.

The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity, taking into account the latest technological trends of 2024–2026. The main possibilities of applying AI to protect information systems are studied: automatic detection of threats and anomalies, real-time incident response, prediction and prevention of cyberattacks, recognition of malicious code and phishing, and continuous learning and adaptation of defense systems. Particular attention is paid to the phenomenon of autonomous AI agents as a new stage in the evolution of intelligent cyber defense systems: practical cases of agentic incident triage and investigation systems (Microsoft Security Copilot), autonomous vulnerability discovery (Google Big Sleep), autonomous penetration testing (XBOW, PentestGPT), as well as the first documented case of an AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign are analyzed. The risks and challenges associated with the use of AI are considered: misuse of technologies by attackers, false positives and missed threats, vulnerabilities of machine learning models and agentic systems, and ethical and legal aspects. The necessity of a balanced approach combining automated AI systems with expert human control based on human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop models is substantiated.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied across finance, including fraud detection, risk assessment, and forecasting, yet forecasting and internal controls are often governed in separate initiatives. This paper examines two pillars of AI use in finance: AI-driven financial modeling and forecasting, and AI-driven reconciliation within internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The paper is based on a literature review of 23 academic, regulatory, and standards sources, including materials from the SEC, PCAOB, and COSO. The review indicates that the two pillars are interdependent: reconciled, well-governed data underpins reliable forecasting, and continuous reconciliation combined with predictive modeling can support pre-filing risk detection in SEC reporting. Model risk management, explainability, and human sign-off emerge as governance requirements common to both pillars. Building on these insights, the paper proposes a five-stage maturity framework that sequences AI-driven reconciliation ahead of predictive forecasting, together with shared governance practices. The findings suggest that managing forecasting and controls under a unified governance approach offers a coherent pathway for AI adoption in finance. JEL classification numbers: C53, G17, G32, M41, M42. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Financial Analytics, Automated Reconciliation, Internal Controls, AI-Driven Finance.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, is rapidly transforming medical education, particularly anatomy, assessment, and simulation.Objective: To systematically review the applications, educational benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and emerging trends of AI in medical education since 2023.Methods: A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and major medical-education publishers for studies published from January 2023 to July 2026.Twenty-nine eligible studies were synthesised across seven thematic domains.Results: AI applications included large language models, anatomy education tools, virtual simulation, AI-assisted assessment, and personalised learning.Evidence suggests potential benefits in learning support, simulation, question generation, and anatomy education.However, concerns regarding accuracy, hallucination, bias, academic integrity, privacy, and inadequate AI literacy remain.Evidence for improved educational outcomes is still limited, with many studies being small, single-centre, or pilot investigations.Conclusion: AI is becoming an important component of medical education, with particularly promising applications in anatomy and pre-clinical teaching.Responsible integration requires faculty oversight, competency-based AI literacy, ethical governance, validation of AI-generated educational content, and stronger outcome-based research.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We evaluated the transformative impact of AI modalities on clinical practice, distinguishing between retrospective algorithmic performance and prospective clinical effectiveness. METHODS: Comprehensive searches were executed [databases searched: January 2016 to October 2024] across PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and Web of Science, identifying peer-reviewed original research and clinical trials. Non-peer-reviewed materials and commercial web sources were strictly excluded. RESULTS: AI technologies-particularly deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and foundation models-demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy in retrospective cohorts across radiology, dermatology, and pathology. In precision therapeutics, AI accelerates drug discovery and facilitates multi-omics integration for individualized treatment planning. Furthermore, autonomous AI systems have proven cost-effective in nationwide diabetic retinopathy screening programs. However, significant gaps remain between in-silico success and real-world clinical utility. Primary barriers include the lack of prospective randomized trials, pervasive risks of algorithmic bias threatening health equity, the "black box" nature of deep neural networks, and stringent interoperability challenges. CONCLUSION: AI serves as a potent computational catalyst for advancing personalized medicine. To transition from retrospective experimental success to standard-of-care clinical integration, future research endeavors must prioritize Explainable AI (XAI), federated learning frameworks for privacy preservation, and rigorous prospective clinical validation under standardized regulatory oversight.
